summary: Describes the design principles behind the Blocks eXtensible eXchange Protocol, BXXP, and more broadly how to design application protocols. It discusses common problems every new protocol must solve, such as framing, authentication, and multiplexing.

eli5.summary: It is a list of the things you must decide when inventing a new language for computers, such as how to start and stop a sentence.

questions: how to design an application protocol
subtitle: Design principles for building generic application protocols that handle asynchronous message exchange.

tldr.problem: When designing application protocols, engineers keep solving the same problems over and over: how to frame messages, how to handle errors, how to do authentication, and how to allow multiple independent exchanges. There are no clear reusable patterns, so every new protocol invents its own answers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3117 describes BXXP (Blocks eXtensible eXchange Protocol), a framework that solves all these common problems once: framing with octet-counting, MIME encoding, 3-digit error codes, channels for asynchrony, SASL for authentication, and TLS for privacy. New protocols can then focus on their unique problem domain instead of reinventing these mechanisms.
tldr.outcome: BXXP was later renamed BEEP and became the basis for several production protocols like reliable syslog. The design principles have influenced how other protocols are built, encouraging reuse and consistency.

today: RFC 3117 remains an Informational RFC describing the design principles behind BEEP (formerly BXXP). BEEP was adopted by the IETF and is used as the framework for several operational protocols, most notably reliable syslog (RFC 3195). The design principles continue to influence how new application protocols are created.

sections.title: Introduction: A Problem Nineteen Years in the Making
sections.content:
SMTP, published in 1981, is nearly perfect: it solves an important problem simply, and the specification is clear and self-contained. Yet in the 19 years since SMTP, dozens of application protocols have been designed for the Internet, and they rarely share code or architecture.

The RFC uses SMTP as a starting point, explaining that when you need an application protocol, you have four options: find an existing protocol that almost fits, layer on top of HTTP, layer on top of email, or design something new. The authors of BXXP evaluated each option for their use case (exchanging Blocks with asynchronous server-initiated messages) and found that none of the existing approaches was a good fit. HTTP and FTP had inflexible framing mechanisms, and email's store-and-forward model was too slow. So they designed BXXP from scratch, but with a goal: make it a reusable framework, not just another one-off protocol.
sections.eli5: For almost 20 years, each new protocol designer said 'I'll just invent my own way to do this.' This RFC asks: why not share a common framework so everyone can focus on their unique part of the problem?

sections.title: Core Concepts: Limiting the Problem
sections.content:
BXXP focuses on three specific kinds of protocols: connection-oriented (like TCP, not connectionless like DNS), message-oriented (exchanging structured data between loosely-coupled systems, not remote procedure calls), and supporting asynchronous message exchange (not just simple request-response).

This scope excludes DNS (connectionless), NFS (tightly-coupled RPC), and multicast applications, but it covers a huge range of real-world protocols including email, file transfer, remote shell, and the world-wide web.

The RFC emphasizes that good architecture "tells you what you can't do." By saying BXXP is not for every kind of protocol, the authors could keep the design simple and focused. This principle—solving a smaller problem well rather than trying to solve everything poorly—runs through the entire RFC.
sections.eli5: Instead of trying to be everything to everyone, BXXP says 'we're really good at this specific kind of problem' and does it well. It's like a specialized tool instead of a broken Swiss Army knife.

sections.title: The Common Problems Every Protocol Must Solve
sections.content:
The RFC identifies six areas that every application protocol must address. Framing tells where one message ends and the next begins; BXXP uses octet-counting (put the size in the header) because it is faster than octet-stuffing (like SMTP's dot-escaping) and avoids FTP's cost of opening new connections.

Encoding defines how messages are represented in bytes. BXXP uses MIME (the same format as email and HTTP), defaulting to XML for human readability and extensibility.

Reporting conveys error information. BXXP borrows SMTP's three-digit reply codes (where the first digit indicates success or failure, the second indicates the subsystem, and the third indicates the specific condition) plus a localized textual diagnostic.

Asynchrony allows independent exchanges over one connection. BXXP introduces channels: each message goes on a numbered channel, and each channel can carry independent exchanges, allowing parallelism while keeping each channel's messages in order.

Authentication verifies peer identity. BXXP uses SASL (Simple Authentication and Security Layer), a framework that lets you plug in different mechanisms like OTP or Kerberos.

Privacy protects against eavesdropping and tampering. BXXP uses TLS (formerly SSL), the same standard that HTTPS uses.
sections.eli5: Six things every protocol does: chop messages up (framing), write them down (encoding), say when things go wrong (reporting), let multiple things happen at once (asynchrony), prove who you are (authentication), and keep secrets (privacy). BXXP does all six in standard, proven ways.

sections.title: Design Principles: Scalability, Efficiency, Simplicity, and Robustness
sections.content:
Beyond the six core problems, the RFC articulates design principles for good protocols. Scalability means the protocol should work well whether there are few or many participants. Protocols that lack asynchrony force applications to open multiple connections, which wastes TCP resources and confuses both the network and the server about how many independent users there are.

Efficiency means avoiding unnecessary overhead. BXXP's octet-counting framing is less elegant than octet-stuffing but much faster in practice. This shows the willingness to trade elegance for performance.

Simplicity and extensibility sometimes clash with efficiency. BXXP uses textual MIME headers even though a binary format would be more compact, because textual headers are easier to understand, debug, and extend. The RFC compares this to SNMP's choice of ASN.1: not the most efficient, but acceptable because the developer community already understands it.

Robustness requires explicit consistency checks even when they add overhead. The RFC warns against Postel's famous robustness principle ('be liberal in what you accept') because accepting slightly-wrong implementations early lets those bugs propagate into the deployed base. It is better to be strict and catch errors early.
sections.eli5: A good protocol scales (works for one user or a million), is efficient (does not waste time), is simple (people can understand it), and is robust (catches mistakes early instead of letting them spread).

sections.title: The BXXP Framework: Putting It Together
sections.content:
BXXP combines all these ideas: octet-counting framing with a MIME payload defaulting to XML, 3-digit codes with localized diagnostics, channels for asynchrony, SASL for authentication, and TLS for privacy. A BXXP session begins with a greeting on channel 0 (the management channel) where peers announce what profiles (application-specific message types) they support.

The session then goes through a "tuning" phase. If you need transport security, you create a channel to negotiate TLS. If you need authentication, you create a channel to run SASL. Once the session is tuned, you create data exchange channels to do "the useful work." Multiple data channels can run in parallel, with each channel processing messages serially but independent channels not blocking each other. This is the key to BXXP's parallelism: multiple channels over one connection, each with its own message queue.

The framework does NOT include naming and authorization, because no single naming scheme fits all problem domains. Instead, applications define their own profiles (message types) and handle naming and authorization themselves. BXXP provides the pipes; applications fill in the content.
sections.eli5: BXXP is like plumbing and electrical: it handles all the infrastructure (connecting, securing, multiplexing) so application designers can focus on what their protocol needs to say, not how to say it.

sections.title: From BXXP to BEEP and Beyond
sections.content:
The RFC describes how to use BXXP: get the core specification, define your own profiles, and start coding. The IETF formed a working group and made three notable enhancements: the default payload changed from text/xml to application/octet-stream for efficiency, the protocol now supports one-to-many exchanges (one client request, multiple server replies), and the name changed from BXXP to BEEP for more favorable acronym expansion.

A complete application protocol using BEEP looks like: BEEP core + one or more profiles + authorization policies + provisioning rules (like DNS SRV records for discovering servers). The RFC cites reliable syslog as an example: a real protocol built on BEEP that demonstrates the framework's utility.
sections.eli5: BXXP works so well that the internet engineering community adopted it, made it better, renamed it BEEP, and used it as the foundation for real protocols that people use today.
